title: When Everyone on the Team Is Expected to Lead
author: Admired Leadership Field Notes
summary: The piece uses Curt Cignetti's Indiana football turnaround to argue a counter-traditional point about team captaincy. In two years Cignetti has taken a program that had accumulated the most losses in Division I football history to Big Ten champions ranked number one nationally. The usual attribution points to confidence, process, and daily commitment to principles that drive practice and game plans. The authors grant those. They spend the rest of the piece on the less obvious move: Cignetti has no team captains, a practice he has followed at every school where he has coached. The rationale flips a 140-year tradition on its head. Most football programs name experienced, high-character players as captains before the season, decorate them with a C, and send them to midfield for coin tosses and to the podium for media. Cignetti does not. In his view, naming a small set of captains quietly signals to everyone else that they are not one. The alternative is to expect every player to step up and act like a leader, at every position and on every play. He randomly selects players to represent the team in different situations, forcing every team member to practise the behaviour of a leader. The evidence the authors point to is the tone of post-championship interviews. Starters and non-starters alike sounded like captains. From there the piece generalises. The best teams, in sports and in business, are player-led. The coach or team leader still sets strategy, selects talent, and measures progress. But the day-to-day functions of leadership, holding a colleague accountable, comforting a teammate, communicating a standard, teaching a newer member, are distributed across the whole team. When a standard slips, nobody waits for the coach. Belief and expectation, the authors argue, are the mechanisms. Tell people they are leaders, then demand the behaviour, and the behaviour follows.
points: The central argument of this piece is grounded in the author's engagement with how real people think and act, not in idealized or abstract reasoning.
The takeaway is actionable,it can be implemented at the classroom or school level without waiting for policy change or external resources.
The piece challenges a common default assumption in education practice and offers a concrete alternative framed by evidence or lived experience.
The stakes are clear: what happens if leaders or teachers adopt this approach, and what is the cost of continuing the current default.
quotes: In just two years under the leadership of Coach Curt Cignetti, the program went from accumulating the most losses in Division I football history to a team that has a solid chance to win the national championship.

Many factors stand out about Cignetti’s coaching philosophy. His unflappable confidence both in himself and in his players pushes the team to reject self-imposed limitations on what can be achieved. He believes in a process that follows Structure, Commitment, and Discipline, using those elements to drive his practices, game plans, and coaching.

Indiana Football has traditionally named team captains on every team since 1952 and in all but five seasons since 1885. Teams across the football landscape share that same tradition. But since Coach Cignetti has arrived, team captain recognition has been discarded. There are no team captains on Indiana’s football team.

In Cignetti’s view, everyone on the team must step up and act like a leader. Leadership must take place all over the field, at every position, and on every play. Every player must play, stand out, and represent the team as a leader and captain.

Cignetti randomly selects players to represent the team in different situations, asking each team member to project the behaviors of a leader. The effect of this philosophy and choice can be heard in the player interviews that followed the Big 10 Championship game. Players across the team, starters and non-starters alike, all acted and sounded like Team Captains.

The best teams in sports and in business are player-led. The coach or team leader sets strategy, selects talent, and measures progress, but they expect everyone on the team to enact the everyday functions of leadership.

When a colleague needs to be held accountable, they don’t wait for the coach or team leader to do it. They step up and act because they are expected to. The same applies to comforting, encouraging, communicating, teaching, and the many other activities that display leadership.

Belief and expectation are powerful motivators in the hands of a skillful leader. Is everyone on your team a leader? It starts with expectation.” Archived from Admired Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
